Question: Is the NASA picture of the M87 black hole credible? 120 AU Schwarzschild radius at 54 million light years distance.
Answer: It is credible, so long as you clearly understand what you are looking at. First of all, it is not a “NASA picture”. It is a picture produced by an international collaboration of radio astronomy observatories. The collaboration is called the “Event Horizon Telescope”, and they spent several years observing M87* to obtain a sufficient amount of data. The picture was synthesized from these observations. These radio telescopes, far apart, formed effectively a single instrument using a technique called very long baseline interferometry (VLBI). Basically, the radio telescopes received signals from the same source, and these signals were then phase coherently recombined. The recombined signal was than fitted against various source models, including models of the M87 black hole as well as alternatives. The best-fit model wins! With the help of this model, the radio astronomy data was then processed to form an image. The image depicts “light” (radio waves) generated in the vicinity of and behind the black hole, partially obscured by the black hole’s so-called photon sphere. The result is the famous synthesized image, its color chosen for purely artistic reasons. So it is an image that is a result of credible science. But no, it is not a NASA image. Nor is it an actual photograph: the image was synthesized using a very complex set of methods, processing several years’ worth of observations made by a worldwide collaboration of radio telescopes. And there is certainly plenty of room there for knowledgeable criticism of the observations, their interpretations, the models and the methods. Question: Would the first light in the universe early on "at average" traverse distances at another rate than now, because of the more frequent bending by gravity in a denser universe?
Answer: No, there would be no significant “bending” except for light rays that happen to pass too close to massive, compact mass concentrations too often. In terms of the average, it’s helpful to keep in mind that what dominates gravity in the nonrelativistic limit is time dilation, not the change in spatial geometry. A light ray coming from the surface of a compact, massive object will appear redshifted to an observer in space, because clocks on that surface tick slower than identical clocks in deep space. Similarly, light coming from the distant past appears redshifted, in part, because the average gravitational field was greater back when matter was much denser. (Another reason is the Doppler redshift due to the rate of expansion itself, but at deep cosmological distances, time dilation dominates over Doppler.) As to the matter of distances, that concept becomes very tricky on its own right! When objects are nearby and their distance remains unchanged or changes slowly, we can measure that distance more or less directly by the exchange of light rays. But over cosmological distances, that is not necessarily possible even in principle; you may send a light ray to a high-redshift, distant galaxy, but you will never observe that light ray catch up with that galaxy, so there will be no response. In the absence of such a direct measurement even in the form of a thought experiment, we must resort to other definitions of “distance”: e.g., distance deduced from the luminosity of the object or distance deduced from the angular size of that object. These inferred quantities are at best poor substitutes for what you or I would consider “distance” in our intuition. In light of this perhaps it makes a tad more sense when someone tells you that, e.g., a high-redshift galaxy was “only” a few billion light years from here when its light was emitted; that light nonetheless traveled for more than ten billion years (so the “light travel distance” is in excess of ten billion light years); and that at the present day, the so-called “comoving distance” to that object is several ten billion light years. All these numbers are valid; none of these numbers describe an ordinary, “sensible” distance, as no such distance can be measured. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: How does semiclassical gravity work and why does it not break down at the Planck length?
Answer: Semiclassical gravity amounts to the idea that we keep gravity classical, but describe matter using quantum field theory on the metrical background of gravity; we then use the expectation value of the stress-energy-momentum tensor in Einstein’s field equations, i.e., we write R μ ν + 1 2 R g μ ν = 8 π G ⟨ T ⟩ μ ν . Now this equation does not care about the Planck scale. The underlying quantum field theory may or may not work at or beyond the Planck scale, but if it does not, that’s not semiclassical gravity’s fault. It is generally assumed that gravity is a quantum field theory, and therefore, using the classical term on the left-hand side of the field equations is not going to work at or beyond the Planck scale, where quantum gravity becomes significant or dominant. But we don’t know this. Perhaps this ugly hybrid works across all scales! Another potential objection is that semiclassical gravity is at odds with the concept of wavefunction collapse. However, this objection is valid only if we treat wavefunction collapse as a physical process, as opposed to a mere mathematical convenience. This, really is the problem with gravity. Semiclassical gravity works a little too well. There are no observational clues that would a) invalidate it and b) point is in the right direction towards a better theory. The problem of quantum gravity is often described as some kind of fundamental incompatibility between general relativity and quantum field theory. That’s not exactly true; we can resolve this incompatibility in different ways. But which way? Without observational clues, we’re groping in the blind. Question: Could you surround an object with gravity sensors so small and accurate that you could have an exact 4D map of the object down to the atomic level, with 3 spatial dimensions and 1 time dimension. For example, could you copy a human brain like this?
Answer: There is no conceivable sensor that would come even close. We are talking about a difference measured in dozens of magnitudes when it comes to what sensors can measure vs. the gravitational field at the atomic level. Having said that, in principle, it would certainly be possible to map an object like that. In fact we’ve done this, sort of. Satellite experiments like GRACE (Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment) have used nothing more than the varying distance between a pair of satellites orbiting the Earth to map the gravitational field of the Earth with exquisite precision, coming up with maps in which the main geographic features of the Earth are recognizable! Unfortunately almost all — scratch that, make it all images that I can find already have the contours of the continents helpfully predrawn, making it hard to discern how much of it we could infer from the observed gravitational anomalies alone. Anyhow, here’s one example: So there, a rather simple “gravity sensor” (again, two satellites connected by a microwave or laser link) mapping the Earth in three, even four (GRACE was able to track changes in the gravitational field over time, e.g., as a result of seasonal ice cover) dimensions. The catch? The ratio of the mass of the Earth vs. the mass of a single proton is a 52-digit number. So no, I don’t think anyone’s brain will be mapped anytime soon at the atomic level using gravity sensors. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: Can you explain the concept of dark energy in the Big Bang theory? Is it considered a part of inflation?
Answer: Not precisely part of inflation, but related. The standard cosmological model assumes a universe that is the same everywhere (homogeneous) and has no preferred direction (isotropic). All forms of “matter” (and by “matter”, we mean anything and everything that’s not empty space) would be in the form of “isotropic perfect fluids”: that is to say, mediums that are characterized by its mass density ρ and pressure p . The ratio of energy density and pressure is a pure number: w = p / c 2 ρ . This “equation of state” characterizes the medium. The number w can be anything between -1 and +1 (yes, this includes negative pressure). It is substantially different from zero only for “relativistic” forms of matter: ordinary matter is well described by w = 0 , which is to say, its pressure is much, much less than its energy density. (Values below -1 would yield an unstable universe; values over +1 would yield a speed of sound that exceeds the vacuum speed of light, violating causality.) So then, the question becomes: What mixture of such perfect fluids yield the observed properties of the universe? When we take the totality of observations into account, we find that observable results — including the cosmic microwave background, its minute fluctuations, the large-scale distribution of matter, the luminosity-redshift relationship of Type Ia supernovae, and a host of other observations — can be best modeled if the universe is assumed to be “spatially flat”, with 30% of all matter in the form of w = 0 “dust”, and 70% in the form of w = − 1 “dark energy”. Ordinary matter amounts to only about 4%, so the remaining 26% of “dust” is assumed to be something invisible, dubbed “dark matter”. Though there are plenty of theories, we have no idea what either of these “dark” things really are; the names are basically placeholders representing our ignorance. There is a curious point concerning matter with significant, relativistic pressure. For ordinary matter, its gravitation is determined by the mass density ρ . However, when relativistic pressure is present, it must be included as a source of gravitation: we end up with ρ + 3 p / c 2 as the source. For dark energy, w = − 1 , this implies that gravitation will be proportional to − 2 ρ , that is to say, it is repulsive! This is why the presence of dark energy actually pushes stuff in distant parts of the universe away from each other, accelerating the rate at which the universe continues to expand. Note that this is not inflation. However, inflation is related. It was supposed to happen in the very early universe, when something akin to dark energy dominated the universe, accelerating its expansion for a very brief but significant period of time. Whatever was the source of that large negative pressure, however, is supposed to have undergone some kind of phase transition, its negative pressure vanishing. Afterwards, the rate of expansion began to decrease and continued to decrease for roughly 9 billion years, before (ordinary and dark) matter became sufficiently dilute so that dark energy became dominant, and the rate of expansion began to increase again. Bottom line: though the mechanisms are closely related, do not confuse inflation (rapid expansion in the extreme early universe) with acceleration (the universe slowly shifting from a decelerating to an accelerating rate of expansion in the past 4–5 billion years).
